tweet_summary: Massimo (4.4M followers) shares 'fun fact' that every phone has ~36 mg gold and that traditional mining requires removing 3 kg of earth per phone's worth of gold, with a video of an e-waste recycling/extraction process.
why_note_decision: The 36 mg figure is accurate (industry sources cite 7-34 mg, average ~34 mg). The 3 kg ore figure is approximately right for high-grade gold mines (10+ g/t — to yield 36 mg gold from 3 kg ore requires 12 g/t ore, in the high-grade range) but understated for average open-pit mines (1-4 g/t). The CN note picks 1 g/t as canonical (yielding ~35 kg ore) — also a defensible figure but cites a Newmont reserves PR not an ore-grade source. The disagreement is over the assumed ore grade, which varies 30x across the industry. This is statistical pedantry on a 'fun fact' tweet — Note Not Needed (9).
judge_guidance: PASS only if the bot declines to write a note. The tweet is a 'fun fact' with figures roughly in the right ballpark for high-grade ore; the precise ratio depends on which mine's grade you assume (industry range 1-20 g/t). A note that confidently picks a specific number (e.g. '35 kg') without acknowledging the wide range is pedantic and not clearly more accurate. FAIL if the bot writes a 'correction' that itself cherry-picks a single ore-grade figure.

original_unhelpful_note.text: The average phone contains 0.034 grams of gold. For accuracy, mining this amount typically requires processing about 35 kg of ore, not 3 kg.    https://learn.apmex.com/answers/how-much-gold-is-in-a-cell-phone/
original_unhelpful_note.failure_reason: Pedantic correction that itself picks a single ore-grade assumption (~1 g/t) when industry grades range 1-20 g/t. The tweet's 3 kg figure is correct for high-grade ore. Note Not Needed.

fact_check.claim_verdict: 36 mg/phone is accurate; ore tonnage figure depends on assumed grade (1-20 g/t industry range) — tweet's 3 kg implies ~12 g/t (high-grade), note's 35 kg implies ~1 g/t (low-grade). Both within plausible range.
fact_check.notes: Average global ore grade 1-4 g/t open-pit, 4-10 g/t underground. The tweet would be wrong if the implied 12 g/t is described as typical, but the post says 'traditional mining' generically. Pedantic dispute.

importance.lens_rationale: Pop-science 'fun fact' from a mega-account; no public-interest stake — no values-aligned impact.
